title: A separated run of text becomes text you can retype
goal: Once text is on its own layer, the natural next thing is to change the words. Turn a separated run into a real text layer with the font, size and colour guessed from the picture, so you can retype a label instead of covering it up. Where the guess is not good enough to look right, the run stays a picture.
notes:
The other stretch, and the first slice in this set where Vision earns its place: VNRecognizeTextRequest gives the actual characters and their boxes on device, which is what this needs and what the geometric detectors cannot provide. The app has no Vision usage today, so this task introduces it; keep it behind this feature rather than threading it through anything else.

Be honest about the hard part. Reading the words is the easy half and macOS does it well. Matching the FACE is the half that decides whether this is delightful or uncanny, and there is no font identification API: the realistic answer is to match against the small set of faces a Mac screenshot actually contains, starting with the system font at the measured weight, and to decline when the match is poor. A retyped label in the wrong font is the kind of thing that makes a person distrust the whole feature, so declining has to be a real, common, unembarrassing outcome.

The user did not ask for this. It follows from what they did ask for, so it is filed last and may well be dropped after the audit on the slices above.

---
SHARED CONTEXT for the Separate into Layers set (asked for by the user on 2026-09-12).

The user's words: "Often I take a screenshot and want to layerize the pieces, so that i can move them around. I wish there was a way to intelligently layerize the parts of the ux. A label, a text run, a box. If there's text in a box, I wish they were heirarchically organize in the layers. I would love somewhere to be an auto layerize feature, but i don't know where. maybe right click on a layer (or the bg layer) and select 'Auto separate'? ... If there is text in a black bg, when we layerize the text, the layer behind it should fill the containing area with the best interpolated color match. If we are layerizing a box, we fill the hole underneath it so that moving the box layer doesn't create a hole. There are some edge cases like shadows. If we can extract that as an actual shadow effect that can move with the layer, that would be amazing. But in the worst case we ignore parts that we can't interpret. I'd love this to at least work on text runs, but ideally break things up so i can easily move the parts individually."

Three things the user was explicit about, which are acceptance criteria and not nice-to-haves:
1. NO HOLES. Taking a piece out and moving it must never reveal a gap. What was behind it is filled with the best match the surrounding pixels can justify.
2. HIERARCHY. Text inside a box comes out as a child of that box, not as a sibling in a flat pile.
3. IGNORE WHAT YOU CANNOT READ. A part the app cannot interpret is left in the background picture, untouched and unmentioned in the layer tree. Guessing badly is worse than skipping.

THE BIG REUSE, read this before designing anything. The measure tool already finds UI elements in a screenshot and already computes the nesting this feature needs:
- PhotonzRender/EdgeMapAnalyzer.swift:36, analyze(CGImage) -> EdgeMap, builds the edge map from a bitmap.
- PhotonzCore/ElementBounds.swift:117, candidates(at:in:luma:...) returns "the nested ladder of element rects around point, innermost first, each containing the one before it", and its own doc comment describes climbing from a line of text to its row to its card. That ladder IS the hierarchy the user is asking for, already written and already tested.
- TextLineBounds finds a line of text geometrically, with a gap parameter for what ends a line, and ElementBounds already has a rule (captionHeightRatio at ElementBounds.swift:113) for when words belong to the control wearing them rather than being an element of their own. That rule is exactly the text-in-a-box question.
- LumaField carries brightness.
The gap between what exists and what this needs is NOT detection. It is: sweeping the whole picture instead of probing one point, cutting a piece out, PATCHING what was behind it, and building the group tree.

Do not reach for Vision or OCR in the first slices. The geometric detectors above already find text lines and boxes with no new dependency, and the app has no Vision usage at all today. Vision's VNRecognizeTextRequest becomes the right tool only for the later slice that turns a run of text into an editable text layer, because that needs the actual characters. Say in the audit how well the geometric pass did before adding a dependency.

THE PATCH, which is the genuinely new machinery and the thing most likely to be done badly. Note first that promoteRegionToLayer (PhotonzCore/Document.swift:741) COPIES a region into a new layer and leaves the original underneath untouched: it has never cut a hole, which is why moving a promoted piece today reveals the same pixels still sitting there. Recommended approach, in this order, and the runner should justify what it chose:
- Sample a ring of pixels just outside the piece being removed. If it is near uniform, fill with that one colour. This is the overwhelmingly common case in real UI: words on a solid button, a bar, a card.
- If the ring varies along one axis, fit a linear gradient to it and fill with that.
- Otherwise extend the nearest border pixels inward.
Do NOT attempt content-aware inpainting. On flat UI it is unnecessary, and on a photograph it would invent detail that is not there. Where even the fallback would be a visible guess, SKIP the piece per rule 3 rather than smearing the picture.
WHERE THE REPAIR GOES, corrected by the user on 2026-09-12 after reading an earlier draft of this task: "if i separate text from a box, i know it doesn't affect the layer underneath, I mean that I WANT it to fill that space with the bg color so that the text is on one layer the bg is on the other". So the result is exactly TWO things and not three: the piece on its own layer, and the background layer with the space it came from filled in. Do NOT stack a separate repair layer above an untouched original - that was the earlier plan here and the user rejected it, because it leaves you with a tree that does not match the simple thing you asked for.

That means the background layer's own pixels are repaired, which is a bake rather than a render-time effect. It is still fully undoable and that is the requirement, not non-destructiveness: undo is a whole-document snapshot, the original bitmap stays in ImageStore, and one Command-Z brings the untouched screenshot back. The app already bakes pixels deliberately in exactly this way - Rasterize Layer, and Turn a shape into a picture - so this is a precedent being followed, not the non-destructive rule in CLAUDE.md being broken. Note in the design doc that this is the one place the app repairs a picture in place, and why.

WHERE IT LIVES. The user's instinct is right: the right-click menu on a layer row, which already exists (Sources/Photonz/LayersRow.swift:202, .contextMenu). It also belongs in the Layer menu, where every other layer command lives (Sources/Photonz/EditorCommands.swift:368). It has to be offered on the background picture layer, which is the case the user actually starts from. The user suggested calling it "Auto separate"; "Separate into Layers" says the same thing in the app's own plainer voice. Pick one, use it in both places, and ask the user in the audit rather than shipping two names.

Everything else: one Separate is ONE undo step however many layers it produces (History.perform, CLAUDE.md). The separated layers get names a person can read in the list, not "Promoted Layer" repeated eleven times. Queue-driven app work targets the NEXT release, and a Current change is not finished until Next has it.

Design doc: docs/design/separate-into-layers.md is the source of truth, written by the foundation task and extended by the rest.
acceptance: A separated run can become a text layer whose words match what was on screen, and retyping them looks like it belongs
The size and the colour are read from the picture closely enough that the retyped words sit where the old ones did, compared side by side in the audit
The font is either identified or a stated fallback is used, and the audit is honest about which happened on each test case
Where the result would not pass as the original, the run stays a picture and says why, rather than shipping words in the wrong face
It is a separate step you choose, not something forced on every run, so the first slice's behaviour is unchanged for anyone who does not ask for this
Tests over a fixture capture covering a light on dark run, a small caption and a heading, written first
Audit under queue/audits/ with each case side by side, and anything rough filed as a follow-up

log.note: deps set: text runs and the patch come first
user corrected the repair design: repair the background in place, two layers not three

Adversarial review BEFORE building. (1) Discoverability: after Separate you get picture layers called Text 3, and nothing says the words can be read. Answer: the command sits in the SAME right-click menu right under Separate into Layers, and the reward is visible - the layer takes the words as its name. Deliberately NOT run automatically on every separation, which the acceptance forbids and which would cost a Vision pass on every command. (2) The footgun: the command will be offered on a whole screenshot too. Rather than hide it, the refusal is a signpost - more than one run reads as 'Separate into Layers first, then turn one run into words'. (3) Cut as decorative: italics, multi-line paragraphs, per-character colour, letter spacing. One line, one face, one colour. (4) The thing that decides delight vs uncanny is the FACE, and there is no font identification API. The honest design is a re-render check: set the recognised words in each candidate face at the measured ink height, lay the two masks on top of each other, and take the best agreement - then DECLINE when even the best is under the bar. That makes declining a measured outcome rather than a hedge. (5) Shortest version that delivers the value: recognise, measure height and colour from the pixels, score a small candidate list by re-render, place so the ink lands exactly where the old ink did. No font metric database, no per-glyph work.

Vision spike before designing anything: VNRecognizeTextRequest on the settings-pane fixture reads all nine runs at confidence 1.00 in 0.24s in a plain headless CLI binary, and its boxes agree with what TextRunSweep found. So reading the words is not the risk; matching the face is, exactly as the task said.

Built. PhotonzCore/TextReading.swift is the pure half (the ink mask, the agreement score, the colour, the bar, the fallback rule, the refusal sentences); PhotonzRender/TextReader.swift is the reading half (VNRecognizeTextRequest, measuring the size and colour off the picture, setting the words again in each candidate face, placing the box so the ink lands where the old ink did). PhotonzDocument.makeTextEditable swaps a picture layer to text in one mutation, so one Command Z puts the picture back. The command is Sources/Photonz/EditorState+ReadText.swift, offered as Turn into Text in the layers row menu and in the Layer menu, right under Separate into Layers.

The measurement that changed the design. Identifying the face by setting the words at the DOCUMENT's point size is wrong on a Retina capture, because the system font tracks its letters further apart at label size than at heading size and a 2x capture's document is in device pixels. Asked that way, four of the six row labels on the fixture come back Helvetica Neue and 'Reset' scores 0.76. Asked at the capture's own point size, every run comes back SF Pro and 'Reset' scores 0.92. So the face is identified at the capture's size and the SIZE is matched again at the layer's scale, with a second, lower bar on what actually lands.

Measured on the settings-pane fixture, all nine runs: words read exactly, all nine in one family (SF Pro), heading Bold, the white-on-blue button label #FFFFFF and the eight dark runs #111111, every one landing within half a pixel of where its ink was and within two pixels of its width. Serif and monospace candidates lose by more than the tie margin everywhere. 40 ms per run in a release build.

Adversarial review of the BUILT thing, on the real app through Scripts/playtest/separate-turn-into-text-walk.json. (1) Retyping the heading works and looks right: 'General' became 'Appearance' in the same bold face, size and colour, in the same place. (2) Asking for the words on the whole screenshot says to separate it first, which is the signpost the design wanted. (3) One Command Z takes the retyping back and the next takes the reading back. (4) What is still rough: the weight wobbles on small labels (two of six row labels read Medium, four Regular, each by a clear margin); retyping a label does not rename its row, which is how every text layer in the app already behaves; and a Retina capture cannot be reproduced byte for byte because of the coordinate space. All three are in the audit's rough list rather than hidden.

Filed find-out-whether-a-label-inside-a-group-can-be-d (p2-normal): in the walk, repeated double clicks on a text layer INSIDE a group never open it for typing, while a top-level one opens on the first. Reproduced in the walk only, so it is filed as something to look into rather than as a bug.
